We are beginning scanning and I'm learning as I go what cases to scan, what not, me getting better margin demarcation for you, etc. Certainly I will be on a learning curve for a time. Due to anatomy, I get cases where a vertical preparation (verti-prep or also called BOPT) is optimal.  These are, I know, not always candidates for scanning but it can be done.  You may not be comfortable with this and if so, just tell me--  in the case where a vertical prep is performed and scanned:    You, as tech, gets to decide the margin.  It's not as impossible as it might seem.  1) Approximately a .3 mm margin with 45 degree emergence angle and profile is the goal. 2) Mark a line at the tissue level. 3) Then mark a line below that down into the sulcus 1 to 2 mm, it's more or less give or take, it's not exacting which I know makes dental techs unsettled.  Place the margin line at the outermost edge of the prepared surface where prepared tooth structure is visible in the scan.   Avoid guessing a chamfer; do not convert the margin into an artificial shoulder.  The final margin is to be placed subgingivally, following the scalloping of the free gingival margin.  Some like to say Position the final margin to the most apical point of the soft tissue sulcus on the working model, but not to exceed 1.0 mm or so subgingivally. (The goal is to not impinge on the biologic width).  I would be happy to discuss with you more or if you're not comfortable doing this, I will consider alternatives. I know this seems very foreign to dental techs and their training but the vertical prep is very effective. My goal is not to make your life more difficult as I've been quite pleased with our collaboration and work together.  Regards,   Tim Goodheart DDS
